rationale:
Split into two children. The node is at depth 4, below the limit of 6.

Why split.
- The parent is a conjunction of three claims. Parts (a) and (b) are the same dominated-convergence argument (supplied steps 1-6) applied to two continuous profiles, g = phi and g(u) = u phi'(u). That argument has four ingredients: vanishing off B_S(y), a bound |g| <= C on [0, infinity), measurability, and pointwise continuity. One lemma for an arbitrary continuous g with g = 0 on (T, infinity) proves both parts, so it is a genuinely reusable obligation, used twice here.
- Part (c) is the only differentiation-under-the-integral argument (supplied steps 1-5 and 7). It needs its own ingredients:
  - the chain-rule derivative -s^(-1)(r/s)phi'(r/s);
  - the dominating function (2 C_1/t)|f| on (t/2, S/T).
  It becomes the second, independent child.
- Each child is about the size of an already accepted leaf of the same kind: aal_cfs_cutoff_pairing_continuousAt (about 55 lines) and aal_cfs_hasDerivAt_cutoff_integral (about 145 lines). Neither accepted leaf can replace a child. They assume either a bounded weight with mu(B_S) < infinity or a fixed inner-product weight, and an antitone cutoff equal to 1 on (-infinity, 1].

Parent assembly. No other mathematical work is needed.
- (a) is profile_continuity with g = phi. phi is continuous because it is C^1, and phi(u) = 0 for u > T because then u >= T.
- (b) is profile_continuity with g(u) = u phi'(u).
  - g is continuous because phi is C^1.
  - For u > T, phi vanishes on the open set (T, infinity) around u, so phi'(u) = 0.
  - The instantiated integrand beta-reduces to the parent's integrand, the product of the factors (r_x/s), phi'(r_x/s) and f(x).
- (c) is cutoff_derivative, verbatim.

Neither child restates the parent, and neither solves another DAG node. Both names are unreserved.

subproblems.title: Continuity in the scale of radial-profile integrals
subproblems.statement: Let n and l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), y in R^(n+l), and f : R^(n+l) -> R mu-integrable on the closed ball B_S(y). Let g : R -> R be continuous with g(u) = 0 for all u > T, where T > 0, and let t > 0 with T t < S. Write r_x := |x - y|; the integral is a Bochner integral over R^(n+l). Then s -> integral g(r_x/s) f(x) dmu is continuous at t.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (y : Amb n ℓ) (f : Amb n ℓ → ℝ) (g : ℝ → ℝ) (S T t : ℝ), IntegrableOn f (closedBall y S) μ → Continuous g → 0 < T → (∀ u : ℝ, T < u → g u = 0) → 0 < t → T * t < S → ContinuousAt (fun s => ∫ x, g (‖x - y‖ / s) * f x ∂μ) t
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1-6 of the parent proof (parts (a) and (b)), stated for a general continuous profile g. The parent applies it with g = phi and with g(u) = u phi'(u).

Notation: r_x := |x - y|, B_S := closedBall y S, nu := mu restricted to B_S, and G_s(x) := g(r_x/s) f(x). Since f is mu-integrable on B_S, f is nu-integrable.

1. Neighbourhood. Since T > 0 and T t < S, we have t < S/T. Let N := (0, S/T). It is an open interval containing t, and T s < S for every s in N.

2. Vanishing.
 - Let s be in N, and let x lie outside B_S, so r_x > S.
 - Then r_x/s > S/s > T, because s > 0 and T s < S. Hence g(r_x/s) = 0 and G_s(x) = 0.
 - So, for every s in N, G_s vanishes outside B_S, and G_s = 1_{B_S} G_s.
 - B_S is closed, hence measurable. Therefore integral G_s dmu = integral_{B_S} G_s dmu = integral G_s dnu.

3. Bound.
 - g is continuous on the nonempty compact interval [0, T], so C := max over [0, T] of |g| is finite, and C >= 0.
 - If 0 <= u <= T then |g(u)| <= C. If u > T then g(u) = 0. So |g(u)| <= C for all u >= 0.
 - For s > 0 and every x we have r_x/s >= 0, hence |G_s(x)| <= C |f(x)|.
 - The function C |f| is nu-integrable, because f is.

4. Measurability. f is nu-integrable, so it is a.e.-strongly measurable for nu. Fix s > 0. The map x -> r_x/s is continuous, so x -> g(r_x/s) is continuous. Hence G_s, a continuous function times f, is a.e.-strongly measurable for nu.

5. Pointwise continuity. Fix x. Since t > 0, s -> r_x/s is continuous at t. Since g is continuous, s -> G_s(x) = g(r_x/s) f(x) is continuous at t.

6. Dominated convergence. Apply the dominated convergence theorem for integrals depending continuously on a parameter, for the measure nu, on the neighbourhood (0, infinity) of t:
 - for every s > 0, G_s is a.e.-strongly measurable for nu (step 4);
 - for every s > 0 and every x, |G_s(x)| <= C |f(x)|, and C |f| is nu-integrable (step 3);
 - for every x, s -> G_s(x) is continuous at t (step 5).
 Hence s -> integral G_s dnu is continuous at t.

7. Transfer to mu.
 - By step 2, s -> integral G_s dmu and s -> integral G_s dnu agree on N, which is a neighbourhood of t.
 - A function that agrees on a neighbourhood of t with a function continuous at t is itself continuous at t.
 - Therefore s -> integral g(r_x/s) f(x) dmu is continuous at t.
proof_key_steps: Since T > 0 and T t < S, t < S/T, so N = (0, S/T) is a neighbourhood of t on which T s < S.
For s in N and x outside B_S(y), r_x/s > T, so g(r_x/s) f(x) = 0. Hence the mu-integral equals the integral against nu = mu restricted to B_S(y).
With C := max over [0, T] of |g|, |g| <= C on [0, infinity). So for s > 0 the integrand is bounded by the nu-integrable function C|f|.
For s > 0 the integrand is a continuous function of x times f, hence a.e.-strongly measurable for nu.
For each x, s -> g(r_x/s) f(x) is continuous at t > 0.
Dominated convergence gives continuity of the nu-integral at t. Agreement on N transfers it to the mu-integral.

subproblems.title: Derivative in the scale of a radial cutoff integral
subproblems.statement: Let n and l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), y in R^(n+l), and f : R^(n+l) -> R mu-integrable on the closed ball B_S(y). Let phi : R -> R be C^1 with phi(u) = 0 for all u >= T, where T > 0, and let t > 0 with T t < S. Write r_x := |x - y| and phi' := deriv phi; all integrals are Bochner integrals over R^(n+l). Then s -> integral phi(r_x/s) f(x) dmu has derivative -(integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) f(x) dmu)/t at t.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (y : Amb n ℓ) (f : Amb n ℓ → ℝ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (S T t : ℝ), IntegrableOn f (closedBall y S) μ → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → 0 < T → (∀ u : ℝ, T ≤ u → φ u = 0) → 0 < t → T * t < S → HasDerivAt (fun s => ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / s) * f x ∂μ) (-(∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * f x ∂μ) / t) t
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1-5 and 7 of the parent proof (part (c)).

Notation: r_x := |x - y|, phi' := deriv phi, B_S := closedBall y S, nu := mu restricted to B_S. Since f is mu-integrable on B_S, f is nu-integrable. Put
 F(s, x) := phi(r_x/s) f(x)   and   F'(s, x) := -s^(-1) (r_x/s) phi'(r_x/s) f(x).

1. Neighbourhood.
 - Since T > 0 and T t < S, we have t < R := S/T.
 - Let N := (t/2, R). It is an open interval containing t and contained in (0, infinity), and T s < S for every s in N.
 - The parent's interval (t/2, t_1), with t_1 = (t + S/T)/2, is a subinterval of N. Either works.

2. Vanishing.
 - phi = 0 on [T, infinity). If u > T, then phi vanishes on the open neighbourhood (T, infinity) of u, so phi'(u) = 0. Thus phi' = 0 on (T, infinity).
 - Let 0 < s < R and let x lie outside B_S, so r_x > S. Then r_x/s > S/s > T. Hence phi(r_x/s) = 0 and phi'(r_x/s) = 0.
 - So, for 0 < s < R, x -> F(s, x) vanishes outside B_S. Since B_S is closed, hence measurable, integral F(s, x) dmu(x) = integral F(s, x) dnu(x).
 - Likewise x -> (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) f(x) vanishes outside B_S (take s = t, which lies in (0, R)). So its mu- and nu-integrals agree.

3. Bounds.
 - phi and phi' are continuous, since phi is C^1. Let C_0 := max over [0, T] of |phi| and C_1 := max over [0, T] of |u phi'(u)|. Both are finite, because [0, T] is a nonempty compact interval, and both are >= 0.
 - For u >= 0 we have |phi(u)| <= C_0 and |u phi'(u)| <= C_1. On [0, T] this is the definition; for u > T both functions vanish (step 2).
 - Since r_x/s >= 0 for s > 0, |F(t, x)| <= C_0 |f(x)| for every x.
 - For s in N and every x: |F'(s, x)| = s^(-1) |(r_x/s) phi'(r_x/s)| |f(x)| <= (C_1/s) |f(x)| <= (2 C_1/t) |f(x)|, because s > t/2 > 0.
 - C_0 |f| and (2 C_1/t) |f| are nu-integrable, because f is.

4. Measurability and integrability.
 - f is a.e.-strongly measurable for nu.
 - For each fixed s > 0, x -> phi(r_x/s) and x -> -s^(-1)(r_x/s) phi'(r_x/s) are continuous, because phi and phi' are continuous. Hence F(s, .) and F'(s, .) are a.e.-strongly measurable for nu.
 - By step 3, |F(t, .)| <= C_0 |f|, so F(t, .) is nu-integrable.

5. Pointwise derivative.
 - Fix x and s different from 0. The map u -> r_x/u has derivative -r_x/s^2 at s.
 - phi is differentiable. By the chain rule, u -> phi(r_x/u) has derivative phi'(r_x/s)(-r_x/s^2) = -s^(-1)(r_x/s) phi'(r_x/s) at s.
 - Multiplying by the constant f(x): u -> F(u, x) has derivative F'(s, x) at s. In particular this holds for every s in N.

6. Differentiation under the integral sign. Apply it for the measure nu on the neighbourhood N of t:
 - F(s, .) is a.e.-strongly measurable for nu for every s in N (step 4);
 - F(t, .) is nu-integrable (step 4);
 - F'(t, .) is a.e.-strongly measurable for nu (step 4);
 - for every x and every s in N, |F'(s, x)| <= (2 C_1/t) |f(x)|, a nu-integrable function (step 3);
 - for every x and every s in N, u -> F(u, x) has derivative F'(s, x) at s (step 5).
 Hence s -> integral F(s, x) dnu(x) has derivative integral F'(t, x) dnu(x) at t.

7. Evaluation and transfer to mu.
 - By linearity of the integral and step 2 at s = t:
   integral F'(t, x) dnu = -(integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) f(x) dnu)/t = -(integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) f(x) dmu)/t.
 - By step 2, s -> integral F(s, x) dmu and s -> integral F(s, x) dnu agree on (0, R), a neighbourhood of t. A derivative at t depends only on the values of the function near t.
 - Therefore s -> integral phi(r_x/s) f(x) dmu has derivative -(integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) f(x) dmu)/t at t.
proof_key_steps: Since T t < S, t < R := S/T. Work on N = (t/2, R), which lies in (0, infinity).
phi' = 0 on (T, infinity). For 0 < s < R the integrands vanish outside B_S(y), so mu-integrals equal integrals against nu = mu restricted to B_S(y).
|phi| <= C_0 and |u phi'(u)| <= C_1 on [0, infinity). Hence |F(t,.)| <= C_0|f|, and for s in N, |F'(s,.)| <= (2 C_1/t)|f|.
F(s,.) and F'(s,.) are continuous functions of x times f, hence a.e.-strongly measurable for nu; F(t,.) is nu-integrable.
Differentiation under the integral sign for nu on N gives the derivative integral F'(t,x) dnu at t.
Linearity evaluates this as -(integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) f dmu)/t. Agreement of the mu- and nu-integrals near t transfers the derivative.
